metadata.title: Claude, Deposition Prep.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Take the deposition-prep skill apart in the Teardown register: explain what a skill actually is (one file, read top-to-bottom before Claude acts), reveal the design choice (specification over instinct), and name the trade-off (repeatability instead of judgment). Lands the carry-out that a skill is a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, not new judgment.

beats.narration_text: You'd think Claude knows how to prep a deposition on its own. It doesn't — someone handed it a file of steps and named the file deposition-prep. Let's open the file and see what's actually in there.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude knows how to prep a witness deposition.', hesitates on 'knows', corrects to 'was given steps for', lands the real question

props.text:
Claude knows how to prep
a witness deposition.
What is a skill, really?

beats.narration_text: Hear "Claude has a deposition-prep skill" and your brain fills in courtroom instinct — like it studied a stack of depositions and came back knowing how to corner a witness. That's the natural read.

production_viz.label: SOUNDS LIKE COURTROOM INSTINCT
chips: KNOWS HOW TO CORNER A WITNESS?
production_viz.caption: that's the natural read

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening: nothing in the model changes. Delete the folder and Claude doesn't forget how to question a witness — there was no instinct there to lose. It just stops running that one checklist.

production_viz.label: NOTHING TO LOSE
production_viz.caption: there was no instinct to lose

beats.narration_text: Here's what a skill actually is: one file. Deposition-prep is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — instructions for pulling a witness's documents from the eDiscovery platform, organizing them around the case theory, and flagging impeachment material. Plain English. Written for Claude to read top to bottom before it does anything.

Claude reads the file top to bottom, then executes it — step by step, in the written order. Pull documents. Sort by case theory. Flag impeachment material. No branching, no rewriting the checklist on the fly, unless the file itself says branch.

That makes a skill a specification, not courtroom judgment. They optimized for one thing: the same organized outline, every witness. The trade-off is real — any question outside those written steps, and Claude is off the map.

So deposition-prep never taught Claude how to cross-examine anyone. It guarantees one thing: every run, Claude reads that same file and produces the same organized outline. That's the whole trick — repeatability, not judgment.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, EVERY RUN

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, EVERY RUN
production_viz.caption: same file, same outline, every run

beats.narration_text: Watch Claude produce a sharp outline and you haven't proved it understood the witness — a file can be followed to the letter on a case Claude never really grasped. Watch it produce a thin outline and the skill isn't broken either — the file's structure may just not fit that case. Neither run tells you a thing about judgment.
A skill doesn't teach Claude how to depose a witness. It's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts — the guarantee is repeatability, the same outline every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Pick a task you do the same way every time — an outline, a report, a checklist. Write it as a SKILL.md: plain English, ordered steps. Walk me through exactly what you'll do before you do it. Go deeper: after one run, ask the model where the checklist broke down — then revise the file so the next run wouldn't.

llm_exercise.prompt: Pick a task I do the same way every time — an outline, a report, or a checklist. Write me a SKILL.md for it: plain English, ordered steps, no hidden logic. Then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you'll do, step by step, before you do it.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: after one run, ask the model where the checklist broke down on this task — then revise the SKILL.md so the next run wouldn't hit the same wall.
